title: Power-Up Multipliers
story: In a card game you are building, each player holds a row of power-up cards. Every card has a multiplier: 3 triples your score, -1 flips it negative, 0 wipes it out. Your score multiplier is all the cards multiplied together.

Before each turn the game must discard one card, and it shows, under every card, what the multiplier would be if that card were the one discarded. The game's scoring code only multiplies: dividing the full product by a card breaks as soon as a card is 0.
task: Write withoutEach(cards). Return a list out of the same length where out[i] is the product of every card except cards[i].
Do not use division. Aim for O(n) time.
constraints: The product of all the non-zero cards fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

examples.explanation: Without the 2: 3 × 4 × 5 = 60. Without the 3: 2 × 4 × 5 = 40. Without the 4: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30. Without the 5: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.
Every product that keeps the 0 is 0. Only discarding the 0 itself gives something else: 3 × 2 × (-1) = -6. Dividing the full product (0) by 0 would crash here.

hints: In [2, 3, 4, 5], the answer under the 4 is 2 × 3 × 5. Which of those cards sit to the left of the 4, and which to the right?
Every answer is (product of all cards to the left) × (product of all cards to the right). For the first card, the left side is empty and counts as 1.
The products of everything to the left of each position can be built in one pass from left to right, each from the previous one. The right-hand products work the same way from the other end.

Fill out[i] with the product of everything before i, using a running product that starts at 1. Then walk from the right with a second running product, starting at 1: multiply out[i] by it, then multiply it by cards[i].
bruteForce: For each position, loop over all the other cards and multiply them together.

That is n − 1 multiplications for each of n positions, so O(n²). With 100,000 cards it is about 10 billion multiplications. Neighbouring answers share almost all their factors, and the brute force recomputes them every time. The division shortcut is O(n) but fails on zeros.

js: * @return {number[]} out[i] = product of all cards except cards[i]

tests.note: two cards: each answer is the other card
one zero at the end: defeats total / card

js: let left = 1; // product of cards before i
let right = 1; // product of cards after i
py: left = 1  # product of cards before i
right = 1  # product of cards after i
walkthrough: Removing card i splits the row in two: the cards before it and the cards after it. The answer is the product of the first part times the product of the second. Both parts can be built up one card at a time, the same way a running sum is.
• Left pass, writing the product of everything before each card: out = [1, 2, 6, 24]. (1 for nothing, then 2, then 2 × 3, then 2 × 3 × 4.)
• Right pass, starting with right = 1. Index 3: out[3] = 24 × 1 = 24, then right = 5.

In each pass, write the answer before multiplying in the current card. That is what keeps card i out of its own answer. Zeros need no special case: they simply turn the running product to 0 for everything past them.
solution.timeWhy: Two passes over the cards, with constant work per card.
solution.spaceWhy: Apart from the output list, only two running products are kept.
solution.takeaway: "Everything except position i" is "everything before i" combined with "everything after i". Build both with running totals from each end (prefix and suffix products here, prefix sums elsewhere) and every answer costs O(1).
